headline: Nearly every county moved left, South Texas most of all
dek: Compared with the 2024 presidential vote, 2,673 of 2,775 counties with a count moved toward Democrats, most by about 14 points. The biggest moves came along the Texas border. The one broad exception was Vermont, where a longtime Republican governor won again.
summary: County by county, the 2026 Senate and governor vote ran about 14 points more Democratic than the 2024 presidential vote.

paras.text: On Nov. 3, voters in 45 states chose a senator or a governor. Of the 2,775 counties where those votes have been counted, 2,673 voted more Democratic than they did in the 2024 race between Kamala Harris and Donald Trump. Only 101 voted more Republican. The typical county moved 14.1 points toward the Democrats, and the move was the same 14.1 points when each county is weighted by its votes. Democrats won 237 counties that Trump carried two years ago. Ten counties went the other way.

This compares a midterm race with a presidential one, so each county's move mixes the national mood with its own candidates. The national mood was clear. 62% of voters in this election disapproved of his job as president, according to the voter poll commissioned by the broadcast networks and the Associated Press, NPR reported. About two-thirds of U.S. midterm voters say Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., the AP Voter Poll found.
The border moved first and farthest

Texas moved more toward the Democrats than any other state. Trump won it by 13.7 points in 2024. This year James Talarico won the Senate race by 12.1, a 25.8-point move. Talarico beat Ken Paxton, whose nomination bolstered Talarico's appeal to Republican and independent voters, according to the AP. Texas last sent a Democrat to the Senate when Lloyd Bentsen was reelected in 1988.

Thirteen of the 15 biggest moves toward Democrats on the map were in Texas. Starr County went from a 16-point Trump win to a 56-point Democratic win, a 72-point move, the largest anywhere. Zapata moved 63 points and Maverick 60. Hidalgo, which cast 202,520 votes, went from Trump by 3 to Democrats by 47. Cameron and Webb counties each moved more than 44 points. The Houston Chronicle traced the statewide result to drops in turnout in rural areas GOP nominee Ken Paxton needed to win, and by a shift among Latino voters, particularly in South Texas, where turnout spiked. In our count, those border counties held their turnout better than the nation did. Hidalgo cast 93% of its 2024 vote, Webb 89% and Cameron 88%, against 75% nationally. Writing for Brookings, William Galston said Hispanic voters who had backed tougher border enforcement objected strongly to the administration's policies in the interior of the country.

The other two counties in that top 15 are in southwest Kansas. Adam Hamilton won the state's Senate race by 5.1 points; Trump had carried Kansas by 16.1. Seward County (Liberal) went from Trump by 39 to Hamilton by 13.5, and Ford County (Dodge City) went from Trump by 38 to a one-point Democratic edge. The Kansas Reflector reported that immigration raids in the region drew Democrats were quick to condemn the effects of the raids and paid visits to Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal., and that according to a New York Times voter trend analysis, 75% of Latino voters in Kansas voted for Hamilton.

Florida showed how far the shift went and where it stopped. Miami-Dade went from Trump by 11.4 to Democrats by 7.1, but Republican Ashley Moody still won the state by 2.9. Axios Miami, citing the Miami Herald, reported that Moody beat Nixon by around 4 percentage points in majority-Hispanic neighborhoods. Angie Nixon was the Democratic nominee.
Across the South and the battlegrounds

In Pennsylvania, Josh Shapiro won a second term over state Treasurer Stacy Garrity by 22.1 points. The state had voted for Trump by 1.7, so that is a 23.8-point move. Roy Cooper won North Carolina's Senate race by 19.6 points and Jon Ossoff won Georgia by 18.0, after both states voted for Trump. In South Carolina, which Trump carried by 17.9, Annie Andrews won by 4.5.

Mississippi voted for Trump by 22.9 points. It now shows Democrat Scott Colom ahead of Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 0.3 points with about 97% counted, and the race has not been called. There is no mechanism for an election to undergo a recount under Mississippi state law., NBC News reported. The Brennan Center found turnout especially high in majority-minority counties once covered by the Voting Rights Act's preclearance rule. There, turnout was as much as 10 percentage points higher than in 2022.

Republicans held the deep-red states, by much less than before. Shelley Moore Capito won West Virginia by 20.4 points, half of Trump's 41.9. In Louisiana, which counts its vote by parish, Julia Letlow won by 1.8 in a state Trump carried by 22. In Arizona, Katie Hobbs won by 13.1. Maricopa County, with more than 1.5 million votes, went from Trump by 3.5 to Hobbs by 16.2. The upper Midwest moved less: Wisconsin 8.9 points, Michigan 8.5, Minnesota 5.9.
Where the map went the other way

Vermont was the exception. Harris won it by 31.8 points. Gov. Phil Scott, a Republican, won by 6.6, a 38.4-point move toward Republicans. All 14 of Vermont's counties are on the list of the biggest moves to the right. Grand Isle went from Harris by 21 to Scott by 29. Chittenden County (Burlington) stayed Democratic, but its margin fell from 54 points to 7. Nine of the 10 counties that flipped toward Republicans are in Vermont.

This is not a turn toward Trump. It compares Harris with a first-time Democratic candidate running against a governor seeking his sixth term. VTDigger reported that Scott defeated Amanda Janoo in a race that proved more competitive than most voters would have imagined when Scott announced he would run again. Vermont Public noted that Scott retained his office on a very good night for Democrats in Vermont.

Maine moved slightly right, by 0.6 points, even though Democrat Troy Jackson unseated Sen. Susan Collins. Maine Public noted that in the past, Collins has been competitive in Democratic-leaning areas, drawing split-ticket and independent voters. Outside New England, the biggest move right was in Schuyler County, Illinois. It moved 15.6 points toward Republicans as its vote fell from 3,756 to 2,025.
Who moved: big places and small, red and blue

The charts beside this section show how even the move was. Counties are not voters, and these numbers describe places, not people. Counties under 10,000 votes moved 13.8 points, weighted by votes. Counties of 10,000 to 50,000 moved 13.6. Counties of 50,000 to 250,000 moved 14.4. The 79 counties with more than 250,000 votes moved 14.1. Small towns and big cities moved about the same amount.

The 2024 result made a little more difference. The 1,718 counties Trump won by 30 points or more moved 15.2 points. Counties decided by under 10 points in 2024, on either side, moved about 15.5. The 122 counties Harris won by 30 or more moved 10.6, so places that were already very Democratic moved least. Hennepin County (Minneapolis) moved 3.3 points and Oakland County, Michigan, 3.7.

The county count cannot tell voters who changed their minds apart from voters who stayed home. Overall, 106.2 million votes have been counted, 75% of the 2024 total. Counties where turnout fell below 65% of 2024 moved 11.9 points, weighted by votes. Counties at 65% to 80% moved 14.3, and counties at 80% to 95% moved 14.4. That lowest group includes big California counties that are still counting, such as San Diego, where 68% of the expected vote is in. The typical county moved about 15 points whether its turnout fell a lot or a little. Across all counties, the link between a county's turnout change and its move is weak (r = −0.14). Turnout alone does not explain the map.

The data block has no Census figures, so it cannot say on its own which kinds of people moved. Surveys give some clues. The AP Voter Poll found only about one-third of Hispanic voters say they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago. In Texas, even about 1 in 10 Republicans voted for Talarico, which points to some voters switching sides. A Washington Post analysis cited by Newsweek found rural counties moved more than 15 points toward Democrats compared with 2024.
Still being counted

Some of these numbers will change. California has counted 71% of its expected vote, Los Angeles County 83% and San Diego 68%. It takes up to 30 days for county elections officials to verify voter records, according to California's secretary of state. Maryland is at 84% and Oregon at 89%. Mississippi has not been called. Alaska does not report by county, so it is not on the map. Its Senate race shows a 0.3-point Democratic edge with 74% counted and has not been called. The Alaska Beacon reported that if neither candidate gets a majority, the ranked-choice count may help Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan.
